questions.question: Which is an acid–base conjugate pair?
questions.answer: A conjugate pair differs by one proton: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{OH}^-$.

questions.question: Which change increases the pH of a solution from 3 to 6?
questions.answer: 3 pH units is a factor of $10^3$ decrease in $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$.

questions.question: Which conductivity curve represents a titration of a weak acid (in the beaker) with a strong base?
questions.answer: Conductivity starts low, rises gently as the salt forms, then rises steeply once excess hydroxide is present.

questions.question: Which solution (all at the same concentration) has the lowest pH?
questions.answer: $\text{NH}_4^+$ is a weak acid; the others are neutral or basic salts.

questions.question: Tollens' reagent is added to an unknown organic compound and a silver mirror forms. Which could the compound be?
questions.answer: Tollens' reagent oxidises aldehydes, producing silver.

questions.question: Which must be true for a reaction where $K_{eq}$ is very large?
questions.answer: A very large $K_{eq}$ means products strongly predominate at equilibrium.
options: The forward reaction is extremely endothermic
At equilibrium the forward rate is much greater than the reverse rate
The reaction essentially proceeds to completion

questions.question: Which of the molecules shown is a secondary amide?
questions.answer: A secondary amide has one alkyl group (and one H) on the nitrogen.

questions.question: Cinnamic acid (shown) is the main flavour component of cinnamon. Which row shows whether it reacts with (bromine water at room temperature; sodium carbonate solution)?
questions.answer: The C=C in the side chain decolourises bromine water and the COOH group reacts with carbonate.

questions.question: Which of the molecules I–IV are isomers of propan-2-yl acetate (shown)?
questions.answer: Propan-2-yl acetate is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$, as are I, II and IV; III is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2$.

questions.question: When $0.1\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ solutions of each pair are mixed, which pair forms a precipitate?
questions.answer: Barium sulfate is insoluble.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of compound A?
questions.answer: The longest chain is hexane; substituents are listed alphabetically with the lowest locants.

questions.question: Which molecule contains a carbon atom with trigonal planar geometry around it?
questions.answer: The carbonyl carbon of ethanal is trigonal planar.

questions.question: Complete combustion of an organic compound formed equal volumes of carbon dioxide and water vapour (same temperature and pressure). What is its molecular formula?
questions.answer: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

questions.question: Which equilibrium produces more product (in mol) both when the temperature is decreased and when the total pressure is increased by decreasing the volume?
questions.answer: The forward reaction must be exothermic and produce fewer moles of gas.

questions.question: Polylactic acid (PLA), shown, is a condensation polymer made from a single monomer. How many proton environments would the $^1$H NMR spectrum of the **monomer** show?
questions.answer: The monomer, lactic acid $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)COOH}$, has $\text{CH}_3$, CH, OH and COOH protons.

questions.question: Which mixture produces a buffer solution when dissolved in 1.0 L of water?
questions.answer: Partial neutralisation leaves a weak acid together with its conjugate base.

questions.question: What is $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ in a solution with $[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}] = 2.0$ and $[\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-] = 1.0\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$? ($K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$)
questions.answer: $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = K_a\dfrac{[\text{acid}]}{[\text{base}]} = 3.6\times10^{-5}$.

questions.question: At $25^\circ$C, $K_w = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}$ for water; at $37^\circ$C, $K_w = 2.4 \times 10^{-14}$. What can be deduced?
questions.answer: A larger $K_w$ means a larger $[\text{H}^+]$, so a lower pH.
options: The pH of pure water decreases when heated
The enthalpy of ionisation of water is negative
The conductivity of water is lower at $37^\circ$C

questions.question: At $700^\circ$C: $\text{H}_2 + \text{I}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{HI}$, $K_1 = 49$; $2\text{H}_2 + \text{S}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{H}_2\text{S}$, $K_2 = 1.1 \times 10^{8}$. What is $K_{eq}$ for $2\text{I}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{S} \rightleftharpoons \text{S}_2 + 4\text{HI}$?
questions.answer: Double the first equation and reverse the second: $K = K_1^2/K_2$.

questions.question: $2\text{NOBr(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO(g)} + \text{Br}_2\text{(g)}$. 4.0 mol of NOBr is placed in a 1.0 L container; at equilibrium $[\text{Br}_2] = 1.0\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$. What is $K_{eq}$?

Acetic acid is flammable. For its complete combustion at 298 K, $\Delta_cH^\ominus = -874.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta_cS^\ominus = -2.6\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$. Using this information, explain why the combustion does not come to equilibrium but proceeds to completion.
questions.answer:
$\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta H^\ominus - T\Delta S^\ominus = -874.2 - 298(-2.6\times10^{-3}) = -873.4\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

The entropy term (+0.8 kJ/mol) is negligible against the enthalpy term, so $\Delta G^\ominus$ is very large and negative. A system reaches a measurable equilibrium only when $\Delta G^\ominus$ is small; here the products are overwhelmingly favoured and the reverse reaction is negligible, so it goes to completion.

questions.question: Formaldehyde trimerises in acidic aqueous solution: $3\text{CH}_2\text{O(aq)} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_3\text{(aq)}$, $K_{eq} = 3.0 \times 10^{-5}$. 1.2 mol of formaldehyde is dissolved to make 1.0 L of solution and allowed to reach equilibrium. Calculate the concentration of $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_3$.
questions.answer:
Let $[\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_3] = x$; then $[\text{CH}_2\text{O}] = 1.2 - 3x$.

$K_{eq} = \dfrac{x}{(1.2-3x)^3} = 3.0\times10^{-5}$. Since $K$ is small, $1.2 - 3x \approx 1.2$:

$x = 3.0\times10^{-5}\times1.2^3 = 5.2\times10^{-5}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ (the assumption is justified).

questions.question: Aluminium sulfate has a solubility of 36.4 g per 100 mL. Calculate $K_{sp}$ for aluminium sulfate.
Methanol is manufactured by $\text{CO(g)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{(g)} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{OH(g)}$, an exothermic reaction. Write the equilibrium constant expression.
questions.answer: $K_{eq} = \dfrac{[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]}{[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2]^2}$

questions.question: Methanol is manufactured by $\text{CO(g)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{(g)} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{OH(g)}$, an exothermic reaction. A mixture of CO, $\text{H}_2$ and methanol is at equilibrium in a vessel of variable volume. Referring to $Q$ and $K_{eq}$, explain the effect of halving the volume on the amount (in mol) of methanol.
questions.answer:
Halving the volume doubles every concentration. Immediately, $Q = \dfrac{2[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]}{2[\text{CO}]\,4[\text{H}_2]^2} = \dfrac{K_{eq}}{4}$.

Since $Q < K_{eq}$, there is net forward reaction until $Q = K_{eq}$ again, so the amount of methanol **increases**.

questions.question: Methanol is manufactured by $\text{CO(g)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{(g)} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{OH(g)}$, an exothermic reaction. Using collision theory, explain the effect of increasing the temperature on $K_{eq}$.
questions.answer:
- Higher temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy: collisions are more frequent and a larger fraction exceed the activation energy, so both forward and reverse rates increase.
- The forward reaction is exothermic, so the reverse reaction has the larger activation energy; its rate increases by a greater factor.
- Net reverse reaction occurs: $[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]$ falls and $[\text{CO}]$, $[\text{H}_2]$ rise until rates are equal again.
- Therefore $K_{eq}$ **decreases**.

questions.question: Write an equation for the reaction between sodium carbonate and hydrochloric acid.
questions.answer: $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\text{(aq)} + 2\text{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow 2\text{NaCl(aq)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)} + \text{CO}_2\text{(g)}$

questions.question: 27.82 g of hydrated sodium carbonate, $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\cdot x\text{H}_2\text{O}$, was dissolved and made up to 1.000 L. 25.00 mL of this solution was neutralised by 48.80 mL of $0.1000\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid. Calculate the concentration of the sodium carbonate solution.

27.82 g of hydrated sodium carbonate, $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\cdot x\text{H}_2\text{O}$, was dissolved and made up to 1.000 L. 25.00 mL of this solution was neutralised by 48.80 mL of $0.1000\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid. By calculating the mass of water in the crystals, find $x$.

The graph shows the titration curve for $0.100\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ ammonia solution titrated with a strong acid. Describe and draw the curve that would result if the ammonia were replaced by sodium hydroxide of the same concentration.
questions.answer:
- Initial pH about **13** (strong base).
- The pH falls slowly, then steeply at the same equivalence volume (25 mL), now with equivalence at **pH 7**.
- Beyond 25 mL the curve is the same as before.

questions.question: Explain the term *amphiprotic* as it relates to the behaviour of salts in solution. Use potassium hydrogen sulfate, $\text{KHSO}_4$, and equations to illustrate your answer.
questions.answer:
An amphiprotic species can both donate and accept a proton. $\text{KHSO}_4$ gives $\text{HSO}_4^-$ ions in solution.

As an acid (proton donor): $\text{HSO}_4^- + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{SO}_4^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

As a base (proton acceptor): $\text{HSO}_4^- + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

(Because $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is a strong acid, $\text{HSO}_4^-$ is only an extremely weak base; in water it behaves essentially as an acid.)

questions.question: A conductometric titration apparatus is shown. Ammonia solution from the burette is added to sulfuric acid in the beaker, giving the conductivity graph. Using A, B or C, identify the equivalence point.
A conductometric titration apparatus is shown. Ammonia solution from the burette is added to sulfuric acid in the beaker, giving the conductivity graph. Explain why the curve has this shape.
questions.answer:
- **At A** conductivity is high: sulfuric acid supplies many highly mobile $\text{H}^+$ ions.
- **A to B:** $\text{H}^+ + \text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{NH}_4^+$ replaces $\text{H}^+$ with much less mobile $\text{NH}_4^+$, so conductivity falls.
- **At B** the acid is neutralised; the solution still conducts because of $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ ions.
- **B to C:** excess ammonia is a weak base that hardly ionises, so conductivity stays nearly constant.

questions.question: According to Brønsted–Lowry theory, state the meaning of the term *weak acid*.
questions.answer: A proton donor that donates its proton only partially: only a small fraction of its molecules ionise in water.

questions.question: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of propanoic acid with water.
questions.answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH(aq)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-\text{(aq)} + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+\text{(aq)}$

questions.question: Determine the pH of a $0.100\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ solution of propanoic acid ($\text{p}K_a = 4.87$).
Calculate the pH of a solution containing 4.81 g of sodium propanoate in 1.0 L of $2.0 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ propanoic acid ($\text{p}K_a = 4.87$), stating any assumptions.
questions.answer:
$n(\text{propanoate}) = 4.81/96.06 = 0.0501$ mol, so $[\text{A}^-] = 0.0501$.

Assume the volume is unchanged and that further ionisation/hydrolysis is negligible, so $[\text{HA}] = 0.020$ and $[\text{A}^-] = 0.0501$.

$[\text{H}^+] = K_a\dfrac{[\text{HA}]}{[\text{A}^-]} = 1.35\times10^{-5}\times\dfrac{0.020}{0.0501} = 5.39\times10^{-6}$, pH $= 5.27$.

questions.question: Lavandulol, found in lavender oil, has the structure shown. Give its molecular formula.
questions.answer: $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{18}\text{O}$

questions.question: Lavandulol, found in lavender oil, has the structure shown. Identify its two functional groups.
questions.answer: Hydroxyl (alcohol) group and carbon–carbon double bonds (alkene).

questions.question: Lavandulol, found in lavender oil, has the structure shown. Draw the structural formula of the molecule formed when lavandulol is exposed to excess chlorine gas.
questions.answer:
Chlorine adds across both C=C bonds:

$(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CCl}-\text{CHCl}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(CH}_2\text{OH)}-\text{CCl(CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$

questions.question: Two forms of polyethylene, differing in the extent of branching, are shown. Identify a property that differs between them and explain why.
questions.answer:
**Property:** Type I (little branching) has a higher melting point (also greater density, hardness and rigidity) than Type II.

Unbranched chains pack closely and have a larger area of contact, so the dispersion forces between chains are stronger and need more energy to overcome. Branches in Type II hold chains apart, weakening these forces.

questions.question: With reference to the structural features of the soap molecule shown, explain the cleaning action of soap.
questions.answer:
- The charged carboxylate **head** is hydrophilic and interacts strongly with water (ion–dipole forces and hydrogen bonding).
- The long hydrocarbon **tail** is non-polar (hydrophobic) and interacts with grease through dispersion forces.
- Tails dissolve into the grease while heads stay in the water; with agitation the grease breaks into droplets surrounded by soap (micelles). Their negative surfaces repel, keeping them suspended so they are rinsed away.

questions.question: The structures of three isomeric alcohols, A, B and C, are shown. Which is resistant to oxidation by acidified potassium dichromate?
questions.answer: **Alcohol C** (a tertiary alcohol).

questions.question: The structures of three isomeric alcohols, A, B and C, are shown. Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of alcohol A.
questions.answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}\text{O(l)} + 9\text{O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow 6\text{CO}_2\text{(g)} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$

questions.question: The structures of three isomeric alcohols, A, B and C, are shown. State the type of reaction alcohol B undergoes to produce 2-bromohexane.
questions.answer: Substitution (the OH group is replaced by Br).

questions.question: The structures of three isomeric alcohols, A, B and C, are shown. State the IUPAC name of alcohol C.
questions.answer: 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol.

questions.question: The structures of three isomeric alcohols, A, B and C, are shown. Which has the lowest boiling point? Explain why.
questions.answer: **Alcohol C.** It is highly branched and more compact, so molecules have a smaller area of contact and weaker dispersion forces; the methyl groups also crowd the OH group, hindering hydrogen bonding. Less energy is therefore needed to separate its molecules.

questions.question: Fumaric acid is converted into several compounds as shown in the reaction scheme. Using the reaction conditions, deduce and draw the structures of compound A, compound B and a section of polymer C.
questions.answer:
- **A** (diester, dimethyl fumarate): $\text{CH}_3\text{OOC}-\text{CH=CH}-\text{COOCH}_3$
- **B** (hydration product, malic acid): $\text{HOOC}-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$
- **C** (addition polymer): $-[\text{CH(COOH)}-\text{CH(COOH)}]_n-$

*Note: the school also accepted a 'condensation polymer', but fumaric acid has only carboxylic acid groups and cannot form one by itself.*

questions.question: Fumaric acid is converted into several compounds as shown in the reaction scheme. State the reagent and conditions needed to prepare compound D from fumaric acid.
questions.answer: Hydrogen gas with a metal catalyst (Pd/C, Pt or Ni).

questions.question: Fumaric acid is converted into several compounds as shown in the reaction scheme. Identify the type of polymerisation fumaric acid undergoes to produce polymer C.
questions.answer: Addition polymerisation (through the C=C bond).

questions.question: A dilute solution of an unknown salt contains one cation ($\text{Mg}^{2+}$, $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ or $\text{Fe}^{3+}$) and one anion (chloride, acetate or sulfate). Outline a sequence of school laboratory tests to confirm its identity, with expected observations and a balanced equation.
questions.answer:
Use a fresh sample for each test.

**Cation**
1. Add dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$: a white precipitate shows $\text{Ba}^{2+}$: $\text{Ba}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + \text{SO}_4^{2-}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4\text{(s)}$.
2. Otherwise add NaOH: an orange-brown precipitate ($\text{Fe(OH)}_3$) shows $\text{Fe}^{3+}$; a white precipitate ($\text{Mg(OH)}_2$) shows $\text{Mg}^{2+}$.

**Anion**
3. Add $\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2$ (acidified with $\text{HNO}_3$): a white precipitate shows sulfate (not possible if the cation is $\text{Ba}^{2+}$).
4. Otherwise add $\text{AgNO}_3$ (acidified with $\text{HNO}_3$): a white precipitate that darkens in light shows chloride.
5. If neither, confirm acetate: warm with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and a vinegar smell is detected (or neutral $\text{FeCl}_3$ gives a deep red solution).

questions.question: UV-Vis spectrophotometry was performed on two samples, A and B, giving the absorption spectra shown. If equal volumes of A and B were mixed (without reaction), which wavelength should be used to measure the absorbance of B? Justify.
questions.answer: About **690 nm** (680–720 nm): B absorbs most strongly there and A absorbs almost nothing, so there is no interference.

questions.question: The calibration curves for two coloured compounds A and B are shown. Solution B had an absorbance of 0.400. If it contained a substance of molar mass $617.53\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$, determine its concentration in $\text{mol L}^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
From line B, $A = 0.400$ corresponds to about $45\ \mu\text{g mL}^{-1} = 0.045\ \text{g L}^{-1}$.

$c = 0.045/617.53 = 7.3\times10^{-5}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

questions.question: The calibration curves for compounds A and B are shown. A contaminated water sample containing compound A had an absorbance of 0.80. Can the curve be used validly to find its concentration? Justify.
questions.answer: No. The standards for A only reach an absorbance of about 0.7, so 0.80 requires extrapolation, and linearity (Beer–Lambert law) has not been shown beyond that range. Dilute the sample by a known factor, or prepare higher standards.

questions.question: An unknown organic compound was analysed by mass spectrometry, IR spectroscopy and $^1$H and $^{13}$C NMR (spectra shown; relative integrations of the $^1$H signals are 1.00 : 1.50 : 1.00 : 1.50 from left to right). Deduce and draw the structural formula, justifying your answer with reference to the spectra.
questions.answer:
**Pentan-2-one**, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

- **Mass spectrum:** molecular ion at $m/z = 86$ ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$); base peak 43 ($\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^+$ / $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7^+$); 71 is loss of $\text{CH}_3$.
- **IR:** strong absorption near 1700 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ (C=O); no broad O–H; C–H near 2900–3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$.
- **$^{13}$C NMR:** five signals (five carbon environments); the one near 210 ppm is a ketone or aldehyde carbonyl.
- **$^1$H NMR:** four environments in ratio 2 : 3 : 2 : 3. Triplet ~2.5 ppm (2H, $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{CH}_2$); singlet ~2.1 ppm (3H, $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ with no neighbouring H); multiplet (sextet) ~1.6 ppm (2H, $\text{CH}_2$ between $\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3$); triplet ~0.9 ppm (3H, $\text{CH}_3$ next to $\text{CH}_2$).

No aldehyde proton appears, ruling out aldehydes; pentan-3-one and 3-methylbutan-2-one would give fewer signals.
